## 2

I understand being skeptical of big institutions and manipulated media, but you don't actually need NASA or space photos to see that the Earth is round—people proved it thousands of years ago with basic observations you can verify yourself.

For example, during a lunar eclipse, the shadow the Earth casts on the Moon is always a circle, regardless of the angle or time of night; the only three-dimensional shape that casts a round shadow from every possible angle is a sphere. Furthermore, if the Earth were flat, anyone looking up at night would see the same stars, just further away. In reality, traveling south causes entire northern constellations to disappear below the horizon while new ones, like the Southern Cross, appear—which only makes geometric sense on a curved surface. You can also watch ships sail away on a clear ocean day; with a telescope, you'll see the bottom of the hull vanish below the water line first while the mast is still clearly visible. 

If the Earth were flat, thousands of independent amateur astronomers, commercial pilots, and everyday sailors worldwide would all have to be maintaining an impossibly elaborate secret for centuries.

## 3

The short answer comes down to light playing a game of cosmic pinball with the air!

Sunlight looks white to us, but it’s actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow combined. Light travels in waves, and different colors have different wave sizes. Red and orange light travel in long, lazy waves, while blue and violet travel in short, quick, choppy waves.

When sunlight hits Earth's atmosphere, it enters a thick blanket of gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). The long red and yellow waves are big enough to slide right past those molecules without hitting much. But the short, choppy blue waves smack directly into the gas particles and bounce off in every possible direction—a process scientists call *Rayleigh scattering*. 

When you look up away from the direct sun, your eyes are catching all that scattered blue light bouncing all across the sky. 

(And if you're wondering why the sky isn't violet, since violet waves are even shorter: the Sun simply puts out a lot more blue light than violet light, and our human eyes are much better at detecting blue!)
